questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-(-1)}{0}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-0}{-1}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+1}{0}=\frac{y-1}{2}=-z,
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{x+1}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $x$ component always maintains the constant value of $x=-1:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1+2t \\ -t\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{x+1}{0}$ part and instead write $x=-1,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{y-1}{2}=-z,\,x=-1
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-t \\ y=-3-2t \\ z=4+7t\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-t \\ -3-2t \\ 4+7t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-t \\ -2t \\ 7t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

This implies that the given line passes through the point $P(0,-3,4)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨-1,-2,7⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-0}{-1}=\frac{y-(-3)}{-2}=\frac{z-4}{7}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x}{-1}=\frac{y+3}{-2}=\frac{z-4}{7}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the straight line with the vector equation

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ 9\end{aligned}]
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
questions.worked_solution:
We have the vector equation 

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ 9\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(3,4,-5)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨4,6,9⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-3}{4}=\frac{y-4}{6}=\frac{z-(-5)}{9}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-3}{4}=\frac{y-4}{6}=\frac{z+5}{9}.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-(-1)}{0}=\frac{y-2}{5}=\frac{z-4}{7}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+1}{0}=\frac{y-2}{5}=\frac{z-4}{7},
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{x+1}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $x$ component always maintains the constant value of $x=-1:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2+5t \\ 4+7t\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{x+1}{0}$ part and instead write $x=-1$, as follows:

$$
\frac{y-2}{5}=\frac{z-4}{7},\,x=-1
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14252071/assets/f65a9806a2d6736a9eed283253225f6e5405d3e272f25e9c6a763651a19d0a31.png)

Find a Cartesian equation of the line shown in the figure above.
questions.worked_solution:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(-1,2,5)$ and $Q(2,2,9).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. Let's consider the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ which is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨2,2,9⟩-⟨-1,2,5⟩ \\  & =⟨3,0,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point $P$ and the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$, we have that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the given line is given by

$$
\frac{x-(-1)}{3}=\frac{y-2}{0}=\frac{z-5}{4}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+1}{3}=\frac{y-2}{0}=\frac{z-5}{4}.
$$

But the above equation is problematic because $\frac{y-2}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, in our line, the $y$ component always maintains the constant value of $y=2.$ For example, our two points $P(-1,2,5)$ and $Q(2,2,9)$ both have $y$-coordinates of $y=2.$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{y-2}{0}$ part and instead write $y=2,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x+1}{3}=\frac{z-5}{4},\,y=2
$$
